extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of comparative government and American citizens interested in Swiss cantons
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed historical-descriptive letters outlining the constitutional structures, offices, selection procedures, and social consequences of governance in various Swiss cantons (Uri, Switz, Berne, Fribourg, Soleure, Lucerne, Zurich, Schaffhausen, Mulhouse, Bienne, St. Gall, Geneva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty resides in the general assembly / sovereign city
rubrics_metrics.description: In several cantons the sovereign is the whole country or a single city; 'the sovereignty resides in the general assembly of the country, where all the males of fifteen years of age have a right of entry and suffrage' (Switz / Uri examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts cantons where sovereignty is in a broad general assembly (with male suffrage at specified ages) versus those where sovereignty is effectively vested in a single city (e.g., Berne, Lucerne, Zurich). Age thresholds vary (fifteen in some cantons, twenty-five in Geneva). Where citizens are numerous the general assembly may rarely be convened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power vested in a senate / council of regency / 'little council'
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive authority is typically delegated to a council (called senate, council of regency, little council, or the fenate) composed of a fixed number of members (examples: council of regency of 60 members in Uri/Switz; Berne's little council of 27; Soleure's senate of 35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These executive councils often meet constantly or frequently, administer day-to-day affairs, and are the actual wielders of administration even when a grand/sovereign council nominally holds legislative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative authority in a grand council
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative power usually resides in a grand council (Examples: Berne's grand council of 200 councillors and 99 assessors; Zurich's grand council of 212 (or 262) members; Bienne's great council of 40), which makes laws, treaties, and sometimes decides appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice many legislative powers are delegated to the executive/senate; the grand council assembles on particular occasions and often confirms actions of the little council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple chambers for specialized affairs (finance, justice, police, orphans, war, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantons maintain specialized bodies: chambers of seven, nine, fifteen; councils of justice; council of war; chamber of orphans; consistory; chamber of accounts; secret council; praetorian chamber; chambers for finance, police, and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These subsidiary chambers handle lesser or specialized affairs and provide internal divisions of function; composition and names vary by canton but the pattern of multiple councils as checks and working bodies is consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and eligibility requirements for offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rules include citizenship, membership in particular tribes/societies, and minimum ages (example: to be eligible into the grand council one must be a citizen and at least thirty years of age; in other places males of 15 or 25 have suffrage for assembly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officeholders are often required to be members of specified social groups (tribes, noble families) and to meet age/tenure qualifications; some offices are for life, others for fixed terms (e.g., avoyers for life, treasurers six years, bannerets four years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacancy-filling by a mixture of ballot and lot to check influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Vacancies are commonly filled by complex mixes of ballot and lot (examples: Berne: twenty-six balls drawn, three gold, etc.; nomination by electors chosen by those who draw golden balls; final selection through drawing gold or silver lots and voting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elaborate procedures are explicitly justified as safeguards against oligarchy and undue family influence: use of lot and secret partitions prevents direct control by powerful families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lot/ballot partitions in nominations to guard against family influence
rubrics_metrics.description: In Fribourg and elsewhere candidate names are placed in a box with partitions; ballots are thrown in without knowing name placements and the partition receiving the most ballots yields the chosen name—designed 'to guard againſt the influence of families.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method is presented as an anti-nepotism/anti-influence mechanism where the pool of eligible candidates is small and family dominance is a threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret council for matters requiring secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: A secret council (composition varies: e.g., Berne's secret council: avoyer out of office, bannerets, treasurers, two secret counsellors) handles affairs that 'require secrecy, and some of these are of great importance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The secret council debates and determines sensitive state matters; its membership tends to be senior magistrates and is a mechanism to centralize confidential decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial roles of bailiffs and appeals structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Bailiffs (bailliwicks) represent sovereign authority, execute laws, collect revenues, and act as judges in civil and criminal causes; appeals can be made (e.g., civil appeals to Berne's courts; criminal appeals to the senate), but appellate judges often have ties to the bailiffs, raising partiality concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appointment method (lot vs. election) and the overlap of judicial and administrative roles raise concerns about impartiality—text notes reason to apprehend partiality where judges were or expect to be bailiffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia obligation and requirements for males
rubrics_metrics.description: Every male of fifteen is enrolled in the militia and obliged to provide himself with a uniform, a musket, powder and ball; no peasant is allowed to marry without producing his arms and uniform; annual inspection/exercise and local arsenals maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This civic-military obligation is enforced through equipment requirements and inspections; dragoons are chosen from substantial farmers who must provide their own horses and accoutrements; states maintain funds for short-term pay and arsenals proportionate to population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political seminary ('exterior state') for youth as training ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cantons maintain a political seminary for youth called the 'exterior state'—a miniature of the whole government where young men assemble, go through all the forms (grand council, senate, avoyers, treasurers, etc.), debate political subjects, and thereby train for public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutionalized apprenticeship is described as improving talents by exercise and preparing youth for future public roles; the post of avoyer is eagerly contested among youth in this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patrician / noble family dominance and exclusion of commerce from office
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cantons (e.g., Fribourg, Soleure, Lucerne, Berne) only a small number of patrician families hold public offices, often live 'without commerce, manufactures, or trades,' and frequently forbid office-holders from being merchants; consequence is lack of commerce, limited literature, and social stratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links this patrician exclusivity to economic stagnation, fewer hands for agriculture, population decrease, and the export of military service (young nobles serving as life-guards to foreign princes). The practice is criticized for preserving oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks, balances, and necessary divisions of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Across democracies and aristocracies the people have been 'necessitated to establish orders, checks and balances'—aristocratic bodies contrive divisions of power to 'check themselves from running into oligarchy' similarly to democracies checking anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recurring theme is that any durable government requires multiple orders and balanced divisions (often three powers) to prevent concentration and abuse—practical institutional mechanisms (chambers, lot/ballot, alternation of office) are presented as realizations of this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign alliances/treaty provisions can conflict with republican independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties (example: defensive alliance with France containing an article authorizing the French monarch to interpose mediation or even compel treaty enforcement) were 'manifestly incompatible with that independence which republicans ought to value' and were wisely omitted in new treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cautionary point is that accepting foreign pensions or mediation clauses can erode republican equality and independence; cantons removed such articles to better align with republican principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socioeconomic consequences of oligarchic constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where government is in the hands of a few, commerce and manufactures are discouraged, nobles avoid trade, revenue and office emoluments accrue to few families, cities often decline in population and industry, while many nobles seek foreign military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text interprets these patterns as predictable outcomes of oligarchic institutions: concentration of offices leads to economic narrowness and social habits that perpetuate oligarchy rather than encourage broader civic participation.
